strengths: R2E provides a coherent, relevant contribution to retrieval-based NLP: candidate answers are represented through retrieved evidence, allowing Shapley attribution to the inputs that actually determine the Reasoner’s score. Training with NULL evidence makes the attribution procedure technically well motivated.

The ranking experiments support the method’s usefulness. On Gene Description Facts, uncorrected R2E improves MRR from the MLM baseline’s 0.167 to 0.202, reaching 0.260 with frequency correction. Updating the retrieval corpus without retraining also improves performance on later literature queries.

The clinical evaluation addresses a meaningful application using 5,671 therapeutic hypotheses. Training the literature models from scratch with pre-2005 evidence is a valuable temporal control. R2E preserves the MLM’s clinical discrimination while adding evidence attribution, and its advantage over the genetics baseline persists when evaluation is restricted to diseases with genetic insight.

The paper provides extensive architectural details, hyperparameters, attribution pseudocode, prompts, ablations, and informative failure examples. The three released evaluation benchmarks are a useful contribution. Together, the documented method and supported empirical results warrant a focused Findings recommendation.
weaknesses: Reproducibility remains constrained despite the detailed description. The training/retrieval corpus includes commercial literature, entity linking uses proprietary resources, and neither code nor model weights are released. The public evaluation datasets permit reuse of the tasks but do not enable straightforward replication of the reported scores. An executable reference implementation using an accessible corpus would substantially strengthen this aspect.

The explanation evaluation establishes less than the broader scientific-reasoning motivation suggests. Shapley values explain the fixed Reasoner computation relative to its NULL baseline; they do not establish biological correctness or expert usefulness. Human validation involves one expert and only eight query-target pairs per task, while clinical evidence relevance reaches AUROC 0.665 against GPT-4 labels. The auditing experiment also lacks an equal-budget alternative selection strategy, so its improvement does not isolate the benefit of Shapley-based selection.

Clinical labels measure development outcomes rather than confirmed efficacy alone. Appendix P acknowledges that discontinued programs can reflect commercial, pharmacological, or patient-selection problems. Moreover, the pre-2005 temporal restriction is documented for literature, but equivalent restrictions are not established for the genetics associations taken from the 2024 resource or the GPT-4 auditor. These variants should be distinguished from the temporally controlled literature-only evaluation.

Some comparisons do not fully isolate the proposed components. Frequency correction is applied to R2E but not the MLM baseline, although Appendix G explicitly derives an MLM correction; this matters for the balanced ranking benchmarks. A simple semantic-matching baseline on the templated genetics evidence would also help distinguish improved disease matching from benefits of the Reasoner. The small clinical gains from adding genetics (0.632 to 0.633 AUROC) and auditing (0.633 to 0.638) support restrained conclusions about these extensions.

Appendix F contains a correctable theoretical inconsistency. Section 3.4 excludes the positive entity when sampling negatives, whereas the derivation assumes independent uniform sampling over all entities. Under the stated procedure, p_neg(a|q) = (1 - p_pos(a|q))/(N - 1), so the optimal logit depends on positive-class log odds rather than simply log probability. Within-query ranking equivalence remains, but the exact probability and PMI interpretations in Appendices F–G need qualification.
